tool.name: MahalanobisPoints
tool.summary: Calculates a Mahalanobis value at each input point, measuring how far the point's combination of landscape-variable values lies from a multivariate reference mean, scaled by the inverse covariance among the variables.
tool.usage:
The value for a point is the quadratic form D2 = (x - mu)' * Sigma^-1 * (x - mu), where x is the point's vector of landscape-variable values, mu is the mean vector, and Sigma^-1 is the inverse covariance matrix. The reference mean and covariance can be computed from a point sample, or read from previously saved tables.
The output is a copy of the input points, keeping all the original attribute fields, with one added DOUBLE field per selected output value (Mahal_D2, Mahal_D, and/or Mahal_pval). Points that fall outside the extent of any landscape raster, or on a NoData cell, receive a null value.
Predictor rasters always contribute their cell values, never raster attribute-table values. A multiband raster expands to one variable per band. A predictor may instead be a polygon feature layer plus a numeric field.
Environments. This tool honors the Output Coordinate System, Cell Size, Processing Extent, and Snap Raster environments (they define the grid on which the landscape variables are sampled). Other geoprocessing environments do not affect it.
Reference: Mahalanobis, P.C. (1936). On the generalised distance in statistics. Proceedings of the National Institute of Sciences of India 2(1):49-55.
Additional reading: Clark et al. (1993), Knick and Dyer (1997), and Farber and Kadmon (2003) illustrate Mahalanobis distances in ecological applications, including the chi-square rescaling and its normality caveat. For the underlying matrix algebra and computation see Golub and Van Loan (1996), Meyer (2000), and Press et al. (2002).

dialogReference.para: The point features at which to compute a Mahalanobis value. The output is a copy of these points with the value field added; a point outside the landscape data, or on a NoData cell, gets a null value.

The raster datasets that define the multivariate space; their cell values are used (never any raster attribute-table values). At least one raster is required - it sets the analysis grid cell size, coordinate system, and extent.
A multiband raster is automatically expanded to one variable per band, named "raster_Band_X". To leave out specific bands, use the Bands to exclude table below.

Order matters: the variables become the columns of the mean vector and covariance matrix in the order listed (rasters first, then polygons), and the same datasets must be supplied in the same order when you reuse a saved mean and covariance (the Existing tables source); a different order silently produces incorrect distances.

Optional polygon variables. Each row is a polygon feature class plus a numeric field, which is rasterized to the analysis grid using that field. Choose the field from the Numeric field dropdown. Polygon variables follow the raster variables in covariance-matrix order.

param.name: exclude_bands
param.displayname: Bands to exclude from multiband rasters (Optional)

dialogReference.para: Optional. To leave out specific bands of a multiband raster, add a row naming the multiband raster and the 1-based band number to exclude. Add one row for each band you want to drop.
How a raster value is read at a point that may not align to a cell center. Exact (nearest cell) uses the containing cell; Interpolated (bilinear) estimates from the four nearest cell centers.

Exact cell values are more appropriate for categorical rasters, while bilinear interpolation is more appropriate for continuous rasters. Interpolation is rarely appropriate for categorical data unless the categories are at least ordinal, and preferably interval or ratio; it should never be used for nominal (unordered) categories.

param.name: stats_source
param.displayname: Source of mean vector and covariance matrix

dialogReference.para: Mahalanobis distance computation requires a vector of mean values and a covariance table. These data can be computed on the fly from the landscape-variable values at the locations of the current points, or they may have been calculated earlier from another set of points.

If you have precomputed means and covariances, select Existing tables and choose the appropriate mean vector and covariance matrix tables (the variable order is then validated against the tables' stored order).

param.name: stats_points
param.displayname: Sample points for statistics (defaults to the input points)

dialogReference.para: The point sample used to compute the mean and covariance when the source is a point sample. Leave empty to use the input points being evaluated - the common case, where each point is scored by how unusual its combination of landscape-variable values is compared with the average conditions over all the points (a statistical distance, not a distance across the landscape - this is how you spot outliers).

Supply a different point layer to score the input points against a separate reference sample instead - candidate sites against verified nest sites, this year's locations against last year's. The two layers are never connected point-to-point: the statistics points only define the reference mean and covariance, and each input point is then scored against those statistics.

param.name: use_selected
param.displayname: Use only the selected statistics points

dialogReference.para: If checked and the statistics points layer has an active selection, only the selected points build the statistics.
A previously saved mean vector table. Used only when the statistics source is Existing tables.
A previously saved covariance matrix table; its stored variable order is used to validate the variable list. Used only when the statistics source is Existing tables.

Standard (inverse) is the ordinary matrix inverse - fast and exact for well-conditioned data, and the right choice in almost all cases; it fails on a singular covariance (a variable with no variance, or two perfectly correlated variables). Pseudo-inverse (SVD) returns a stable least-squares inverse when variables are strongly collinear. The tool reports the covariance condition number.

Output point feature class: a copy of the input points - all the original attribute fields are preserved - with one Mahalanobis value field per selected output value (Mahal_D2, Mahal_D, and/or Mahal_pval). Defaults to Mahalanobis_Points in the current workspace, auto-incremented if that name is taken.

param.name: out_d2
param.displayname: Squared distance (D2) -- traditional for ecological modeling

dialogReference.para: Check to write the per-point squared Mahalanobis distance D2 = (x - mu)' * Sigma^-1 * (x - mu) to the field Mahal_D2. This is the traditional quantity used in ecological modeling. At least one of the three output values must be checked.
Check to write the Mahalanobis distance D (the square root of D2) to the field Mahal_D. At least one of the three output values must be checked.

Check to write the chi-square p-value to the field Mahal_pval: the upper-tail probability of D2 under a chi-square distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of variables. It is a 0 to 1 similarity score where numbers near 1 indicate a point that closely matches the reference conditions. At least one of the three output values must be checked.

Note on degrees of freedom: this tool uses the statistically standard value, df = number of variables (Mardia, Kent and Bibby 1979; Seber 1984). Some ecological sources instead use number of variables minus 1 (Clark et al. 1993; Farber and Kadmon 2003). Because the chi-square transform is monotonic in D2, the choice only rescales the p-values and never changes the ranking or relative ordering of points.
Check to also write the computed mean vector to a table. When checked, an output name is auto-filled below.
Output table for the mean vector (one row per variable), with the ordered variable list stored in its metadata. Auto-named using the output name plus _Means.
Check to also write the covariance matrix to a table.
Output table for the covariance matrix. Auto-named using the output name plus _Covariance.
Check to also write the inverse covariance matrix to a table.
Output table for the inverse covariance matrix. Auto-named using the output name plus _Inv_Covariance.
Check to also write the correlation matrix to a table.
Output table for the correlation matrix, derived from the covariance. Auto-named using the output name plus _Correlation.

scriptExample.title: MahalanobisPoints example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Compute a squared-distance (D2) Mahalanobis value at each observed location, building the mean and covariance from those same points.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.MahalanobisPoints( target_points="Observed_Locations", raster_vars="elev_clip;slope_clip;curvature", sample_method="Interpolated (bilinear)", stats_source="Calculate directly from sample point features", inversion="Standard (inverse)", out_points=r"C:\Project\Mahalanobis.gdb\Observed_Mahal", out_d2=True, out_d=False, out_pval=True)

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Calculates a Mahalanobis value at each input point from a set of landscape variables and a reference mean and covariance.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Calculates, for each input point, the Mahalanobis distance between the point's vector of landscape-variable values and a multivariate reference mean, scaled by the inverse covariance matrix of the variables. The reference mean vector and covariance matrix can be computed from a point sample, or read from previously saved tables. The output is a copy of the input points with one or more added fields holding the squared distance (D2), the distance (D), and/or a chi-square p-value (a 0 to 1 similarity score); points outside the landscape data are null. Method reference: Mahalanobis (1936).
